claims.text: The investigated material is an equimolar W-Ta-Ti-V-Zr high-entropy alloy.
The WTaTiVZr alloy is single-phase and fully homogenized.
WTaTiVZr is composed of low-activation refractory elements.
Heterogeneous elemental distribution in equimolar WTaTiVZr produces severe local lattice distortions.
The local lattice distortions generate localized variations in stress fields.
The distortion-induced stress fields alter dislocation dynamics and enhance dislocation interactions.
The altered local stress fields facilitate activation of multiple slip systems in WTaTiVZr.
The altered local stress fields promote deformation twinning in WTaTiVZr.
High-temperature deformation of WTaTiVZr produces sub-grain boundaries.
Multiple slip and twinning distribute plastic deformation more broadly in WTaTiVZr than in pure tungsten.
The proposed deformation mechanisms impede crack initiation and propagation.
Distributed plastic deformation delays brittle failure in WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
At 1000–1200 °C under otherwise identical loading conditions, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain than pure tungsten.
At 1000–1200 °C under otherwise identical loading conditions, WTaTiVZr will absorb more energy before failure and exhibit greater toughness than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit more pronounced dislocation and twin structures after high-temperature loading than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten will exhibit lower ductility and toughness and more localized brittle fracture than WTaTiVZr under the specified loading conditions.
Matching grain size and microstructure while applying identical high-temperature loading to WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten provides a controlled comparison of their deformation behavior.

The proposed mechanism is limited to plasma-facing-component-relevant temperature and strain-rate regimes and may cease to apply when microstructural scale or compositional homogeneity changes substantially.
